claims.text: Nanostructuring tungsten increases its grain-boundary density.
An increased density of engineered grain boundaries facilitates grain-boundary sliding in tungsten.
Grain-boundary sliding synergistically enhances thermally activated dislocation climb at high temperature.
Coupled grain-boundary sliding and dislocation climb promote dynamic recovery.
Dynamic recovery spreads plastic deformation more uniformly.
The proposed combined mechanism improves tungsten toughness.
Ultrafine-grained tungsten will undergo more uniform plastic deformation than coarse-grained tungsten.
Ultrafine-grained tungsten will exhibit greater plastic strain or ductility than coarse-grained tungsten.
Ultrafine-grained tungsten will exhibit higher fracture toughness than coarse-grained tungsten.
Ultrafine-grained specimens will show observable signatures of active grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature testing.
Ultrafine-grained specimens will show TEM evidence of dislocation climb and recovery.
Grain-boundary pinning or rapid-heating protocols can prevent excessive grain coarsening during testing.
The mechanism should operate in tungsten between 1200 and 1500 °C under vacuum or inert conditions when grain growth is suppressed.
Oxidation can alter grain-boundary behavior enough to invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Failure to stabilize the ultrafine grains may cause grain growth that confounds the comparison.
The comparison uses ultrafine grains below one micrometre and coarse grains tens of micrometres in size.
The proposed test strain rates are relevant to fusion plasma-facing service conditions.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as processed under identical conditions, but the ultrafine-grained group receives additional stabilization methods. Unless the coarse-grained control receives a matched stabilization treatment, variables other than grain-boundary density differ between groups.
